questions.ask: What do you want to create — a working prototype with no database behind it, the frontend of a new project, or Atoms going into a project you already have?
questions.why: The fork everything else follows from, and the only question about the work that has to be asked outright. A prototype is React with sample data and no backend. A new project gets its stack chosen. An existing project gets an install and nothing created.

React with Vite is the default and the right answer unless something needs a server — auth, data that has to survive a reload, API routes, or a secret the browser must not see. Next is not more capable for the UI, only for what sits behind it.

questions.ask: What is the existing app — framework and version, which React version, does it already use MUI, and is Atoms already installed?
questions.why: Atoms ships MUI and a theme inside it. An app that already mounts its own theme provider has to have that reconciled before anything renders correctly, and React 17 is not supported at all. Finding either out after installing is a rollback. The Atoms version matters for the same reason: the code these tools serve is written against the current release, and an app that installed months ago is on something else.
questions.accepts: framework + version, React major, whether MUI is already there, installed Atoms version (or "none")
followUps: Is there already a design system or component library in it?
Does it already have a theme provider, and who owns it?

What does `npm ls @neofloai/atoms --depth=0` say in that project? Read it from there rather than from the package.json dependency line — a git install shows a commit or a range there, not a version. Answer "none" if it is not installed yet.

questions.ask: Which screens are there? Name each one and say in a sentence what a person does on it.
questions.why: The count and the verbs decide the routing and the shell. One screen with no navigation is a different app from four behind a rail, and finding that out after the shell is built means rebuilding it.
questions.accepts: one line per screen: name — what a person does there
followUps: How does someone get from each screen to the next — the rail, clicking a row, a button?
Is anything on these screens meant to be drawn but not wired, so nobody demos a picture by accident?

questions.ask: Is there an app shell — a nav rail down the side with a bar across the content — or is it a single screen with no chrome?
questions.why: The shell is the arrangement most often built backwards. The rail runs the full height and the bar starts where the rail ends, so the outer box is a row rather than a bar with a row underneath. Answering this up front is what makes the Dashboard pattern usable as it is.
followUps: What are the rail's destinations, in order, and which is selected when it opens?
Does the rail collapse to icons?

questions.ask: If a screen has a table or a list: what does one row represent, and what are the columns?
questions.why: Column widths and whether a table scrolls sideways are decided by the real columns. A table built against invented ones has to be re-measured against the real ones later.
questions.accepts: per table: what a row is, and the column names
followUps: Which columns are statuses or categories worth filtering on?
Which column identifies a row to a person — the thing they would read out loud?

questions.ask: Light, dark, or a switch in the app so the person viewing can change it?
questions.why: Every token carries both schemes, so this is one prop. Light unless there is a reason — and a demo on a projector or someone else's laptop wants pinning rather than a switch nobody will find.

questions.ask: What is it called on screen — and is it Neoflo-branded, or does it carry a customer's name?
questions.why: Decides what sits beside the mark in the rail and what the browser tab says. The Neoflo mark and favicon go in either way unless the answer says otherwise.
questions.accepts: the name shown in the UI, noting whether it is a customer brand

questions.ask: What should the folder be called?
questions.why: It becomes the directory on the Desktop and the package name. Renaming it afterwards means touching both.

targets.label: React + Vite + TypeScript (Atoms template)
targets.chooseWhen: it is a prototype, or a new project whose frontend does not need a server of its own

steps.title: Name it and install
steps.body: The template arrives named `atoms-app` and titled "Atoms App". Give it the project's name, then install. Commit the `package-lock.json` this writes.

steps.title: Read AGENTS.md before writing anything
steps.body: The project's `AGENTS.md` (which `CLAUDE.md` imports) is the structure and the rules for working in it, and they are strict: every file goes in one of four layers, each layer imports only downwards, and oxlint fails `npm run check` on a boundary crossed. `features/invoices` is the worked example — copy its shape for each feature, then delete it, its page and its nav row once the app has its own.

steps.title: Run it
steps.body: Vite serves on port 5173. Leave it running while you build; it reloads on save. Run `npm run check` and `npm run build` before calling anything done.

targets.label: Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript
targets.chooseWhen: a new project was asked for with Next: something behind the UI needs a server — a sign-in, data that outlives a reload, an API route, or a secret that must stay out of the browser

iconStep.title: Declare the icons in the root layout
iconStep.body: The `app/icon.png` file convention cannot express a `media` query, so the icons are declared as metadata instead. One PNG rather than a light/dark pair — the off-white disc is legible on both chromes, and a browser that ignores `media` on an icon link would otherwise show nothing at all.

steps.title: Keep server work on the server
steps.body: Components are server components by default; `NeofloThemeProvider` is a client component and is rendered inside the server layout. Fetch in server components or route handlers, and keep API keys in `.env.local`, which is git-ignored by default. A key read in a client component ships to the browser.

targets.label: A project that already exists
targets.chooseWhen: Atoms is being added to an app that is already running, so nothing is created and nothing is scaffolded

steps.title: Do not create a project
steps.body: Work inside the repo that exists. Call `get_installation` with that app's framework for the install and provider steps, and read the rules it returns before importing anything.

steps.title: Check React first
steps.body: Atoms needs React 18 or 19 as a peer dependency. On React 17 or earlier, stop and say so — there is no workaround, and finding out after the install is a rollback.

steps.title: Reconcile an existing theme provider
steps.body: If the app already mounts a MUI theme, two providers will fight and the inner one silently wins for anything it styles. `NeofloThemeProvider` is the only theme Atoms components are correct under, so either the existing provider wraps a region that excludes Atoms components, or it goes. That is a decision for whoever owns the app, not one to make while installing.

steps.title: Leave the brand alone unless asked
steps.body: A customer-facing app keeps its own favicon and its own mark. Do not replace either without being asked to.

prototype: Every screen has to be reachable by clicking. No sign-in gate, no route that can only be reached by editing the URL.
Assume it gets shown to other people, live. Every click has to land somewhere — a dead control in front of a room is the only thing anyone remembers.

Put the sample data in each feature's `mocks/` folder, in the shape the real API will return, read only by that feature's `api/`. What is on screen changes far more often than the components do, and nobody should have to open a component to change a vendor name — and the day the API exists, switching is one file per feature.
Nothing half-styled. A control that is not wired yet still has to look finished, because in a review it will be read as the design rather than as a placeholder.
Nothing that needs a network. If the room has no wifi it still has to run.
One obvious path through the screens, and the two commands that start it at the top of the README: `npm install`, `npm run dev`. Anything more than that will not survive being handed on.
new-project: Keep the sample data behind the function signature the real source will have, so swapping it later is one file rather than a search.
Type the records properly. A table built on loose rows is a table that will not survive the real ones.
Mark the seams where real data will arrive with a comment saying what is expected, rather than spreading a mock through the components.

Pin the Atoms install to a semver range (`#semver:^1.0.0`) rather than installing bare -- a bare install tracks the default branch, so the version in the project has no name and nothing to compare against. Record which version went in.
Do not wrap or restyle an Atoms component locally to get a variant that does not exist. Open an issue on the Atoms repo — a local override stops tracking the design system the day it is written.
existing-project: Resolve the Atoms version already in the app before writing anything -- `npm ls @neofloai/atoms --depth=0` in that project, not the dependency line in its package.json. The code these tools serve targets the current release, and an app that installed months ago is on something else.
Pin the install to a semver range (`#semver:^1.0.0`) rather than a bare install or a branch. An app already in front of users does not want its buttons changing on someone else's merge.
Introduce it on one screen first. A single screen and a whole-app migration are the same install and very different reviews.
Leave the app's own components where they are. Atoms sits alongside them; replacing what already works is separate work with its own approval.
Do not wrap or restyle an Atoms component locally to get a variant that does not exist. Open an issue on the Atoms repo — a local override stops tracking the design system the day it is written.

rules: Do not scaffold, install, or write a component until every required answer is in hand. Ask the questions in one pass rather than one at a time, and ask the follow-ups for anything that came back vague.

Hold state in React state. Do not add `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, cookies or a database to make something survive a reload unless the user asks for it — a prototype that remembers the last person who used it cannot be reset before the next demo.

Call `get_pattern` before composing a screen, `get_component` before using a component, and `get_tokens` before writing any colour, spacing or type value. Never hardcode a hex or a pixel value that a token already carries.
Import only from `@neofloai/atoms`, `@neofloai/atoms/icons`, `@neofloai/atoms/tokens` and `@neofloai/atoms/theme`. Importing from `@mui/material` resolves and bypasses the design system.
When it runs, say how to see it — the folder and the command for something new, the route for a screen inside an app that already runs. Then say which interactions are real and which are only drawn.
creationRules: Create the project in ~/Desktop/<project-name>. Not a temp directory, not inside the Atoms repo, not whatever directory this conversation started in — a prototype nobody can find again was not delivered. If that folder does not exist, ask where it should go rather than guessing.
If a folder of that name is already there, stop and ask. Never scaffold into or over an existing directory.

brandAssets.note: 16/32/48px copy of the default, for the /favicon.ico path crawlers request directly
Off-white disc with a dark mark. The default: the only file that survives both light and dark browser chrome
Full-bleed square for the iOS home screen, which ignores transparency and applies its own rounding

logoStep.title: Put the mark in the app
logoStep.body: The logo is a component and inherits `currentColor`, so there is no asset to add and no light/dark pair to switch between. It belongs at the top of the nav rail; in a customer-branded app it is their name that goes there instead, and the favicon stays theirs too.

structure.tree:
src/
├── main.tsx              Mounts <App />. Nothing else goes here.
├── app/                  Composition root: wiring, never features.
│   ├── App.tsx
│   ├── providers/        NeofloThemeProvider, QueryClient, Snackbar.
│   ├── router/           Route table. Every page is lazy-loaded.
│   ├── layout/           The shell: rail, bar, <Outlet />, nav rows.
│   └── errors/           Route error boundary.
├── pages/                One folder per route. Thin: composes features.
│   └── <route>/<Route>Page.tsx
├── features/             One folder per business capability.
│   └── <feature>/        See the slice shape below.
├── shared/               Domain-free building blocks.
│   ├── api/              httpClient, mockResponse.
│   ├── config/           env.ts (every env var), paths.ts (every route).
│   ├── lib/              Pure helpers: formatting, dates, maths.
│   ├── ui/               Compositions of Atoms used by 2+ pages.
│   └── hooks/            Domain-free hooks (useDebounce, …).
└── test/                 Test setup and renderWithProviders.
structure.featureTree:
features/<feature>/
├── index.ts              The public API. The only file outside code imports.
├── model/                Types and pure functions. No React, no fetching.
├── api/                  <feature>Api.ts (transport) and <feature>Queries.ts
│                         (query keys + TanStack Query hooks).
├── mocks/                Sample data in the API's exact shape. Read only by api/.
├── components/           The feature's UI, built from Atoms components.
└── hooks/                Feature hooks that are not queries (optional).

layers.owns: Providers, the router, the shell and the error boundary — the wiring that turns pages into an app.
One component per route that lays out the screen and composes features. No business logic.
A business capability end to end: its types, its API calls, its queries, its mocks and its UI.
Code with no domain knowledge: the HTTP client, config, formatting, and Atoms compositions used by more than one page.

rules.rule: Put every file in one of the four layers — `app`, `pages`, `features`, `shared` — in the folder this document names for it. Do not create new top-level folders under `src/` (no `src/components`, `src/utils`, `src/helpers`, `src/services`, `src/store`).
rules.why: A second place for the same kind of code is how two engineers end up writing the same thing twice. One answer to "where does this go" is what keeps a codebase navigable at fifty features.

rules.rule: Import only downwards: `app → pages → features → shared`. `shared` imports no layer; a feature imports only `shared`; a page imports features and `shared`.
rules.why: Dependencies that point one way can be reasoned about, tested and deleted one layer at a time. A single upward import makes the bottom layer depend on everything above it.

rules.rule: Features never import other features. When two features need each other, compose them in a page; when they need the same code, move it to `shared` if it has no domain knowledge.
rules.why: Features that import each other stop being separable — a change to one is a change to all of them, and none can be removed or rewritten alone.

rules.rule: Import a feature only through its `index.ts` (`@/features/invoices`), never a file inside it. Export from `index.ts` only what a page needs.
rules.why: The index is the feature's contract. Everything behind it can be reorganised without breaking a caller — and because `package.json` declares the app free of side effects, a page that imports one hook from the index does not bundle the feature's table along with it.

rules.rule: Inside a feature, use relative imports (`../model/invoice`). Across folders, use the `@/` alias. Never `../../`.
rules.why: The alias says which layer an import comes from at a glance, and it survives a file moving one folder deeper.

rules.rule: Keep `shared` free of business words. If code names an invoice, a vendor or a user role, it belongs to a feature.
rules.why: `shared` is imported by everything, so domain logic there leaks into every feature and is owned by none of them.

rules.rule: Promote code to `shared` on its second user, not its first. Until then it stays in the feature that has it.
rules.why: An abstraction with one caller is a guess about the second. Waiting costs one copy; guessing wrong costs a refactor across every caller.

rules.rule: One folder per route under `pages/`, one `<Name>Page.tsx` in it, registered in `app/router/router.tsx` with `lazy`. Pages do not import each other.
rules.why: Lazy routes keep the first load paying only for the first page. Pages importing pages is how a route ends up bundling three others.

rules.rule: Pages compose: they call feature hooks and pass the data to feature components. A page holds no fetch, no business rule and no data transformation.
rules.why: Logic in a page cannot be reused by the next page that needs it, and is tested only through a full screen render.

rules.rule: Every route path lives in `shared/config/paths.ts`. Link and navigate with `paths.x`, never a string literal.
rules.why: Renaming a route is then one edit, and a typo is a type error rather than a 404 found in a demo.

rules.rule: Server state goes through TanStack Query: transport functions in `features/<f>/api/<f>Api.ts`, query keys and hooks in `features/<f>/api/<f>Queries.ts`. Components never call `fetch` or the HTTP client directly.
rules.why: One cache gives every screen loading, error, retry, deduplication and invalidation for free. A component that fetches for itself gets none of it and duplicates the request the next one makes.

rules.rule: All HTTP goes through `shared/api/httpClient.ts`. Do not add axios, ky or a second client.
rules.why: Auth headers, base URLs and error shapes then change in one file.

rules.rule: Build query keys from the feature's key factory (`invoiceKeys.list()`), always prefixed with the feature name.
rules.why: Invalidating `invoiceKeys.all` then refreshes exactly what the feature cached and nothing else.

rules.rule: Sample data lives in `features/<f>/mocks/`, in the exact shape the API returns, and only the feature's `api/` folder reads it, behind `env.useMocks`.
rules.why: Swapping to the real endpoint is then one file in `api/`, and no component knows the data was ever fake.

rules.rule: UI state lives in React state, or in the URL (`useSearchParams`) when it should survive a reload or be shareable — filters, tabs, the selected row. Never `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` for app data. Do not add Redux, Zustand, Jotai or any global store unless the user asks for one.
rules.why: With server state in the query cache, what is left is almost always local. A global store added "for later" becomes the place everything goes, and a stored value read back at the wrong moment looks like a bug in the design.

rules.rule: Read environment variables only from `shared/config/env.ts`. A new variable is declared in three places: `env.ts`, `src/vite-env.d.ts` and `.env.example`. Never put a secret in a `VITE_` variable.
rules.why: Every `VITE_` variable ships to the browser. One file that reads them all is the list of what a deploy needs.

rules.rule: Build UI only from `@neofloai/atoms`, `@neofloai/atoms/icons`, `@neofloai/atoms/tokens` and `@neofloai/atoms/theme`. Never import `@mui/*`, `@emotion/*` or `@neofloai/atoms/dist/*`, and do not add another UI kit or CSS framework (Tailwind, styled-components, CSS modules for components).
rules.why: MUI resolves because Atoms ships it, and importing it silently bypasses the design system. A second styling system means two ways to draw every control.

rules.rule: Before composing a screen call the Atoms MCP `get_pattern`; before using a component call `get_component`; before writing any colour, spacing, radius or type value call `get_tokens`. Never hardcode a hex or pixel value a token carries.
rules.why: A pattern carries an arrangement that has already been reviewed, and a component's Related section says when a different one is right. Hardcoded values stop following the theme, including dark mode.

rules.rule: Use Atoms components unmodified. No `sx` selector reaching inside a component (`& .MuiButton-…`), no wrapper that overrides its styles. When a design needs a variant Atoms lacks, use the closest one and report the gap.
rules.why: A local override stops tracking the design system the day it is written, and every project ends up with a different button.

rules.rule: `NeofloThemeProvider` is mounted once, in `app/providers/AppProviders.tsx`. Never call `createTheme` or mount a second theme provider.
rules.why: Two providers fight, and the inner one silently wins for everything inside it.

rules.rule: A component used by two or more pages and free of business words goes in `shared/ui/`; anything else stays in its feature's `components/`.
rules.why: Same rule as `shared` itself — reuse is earned by the second caller.

rules.rule: Named exports only, no default exports (config files excepted).
rules.why: A named export is the same name at every import site, so search and rename find all of them.

rules.rule: TypeScript stays strict. No `any`, no non-null `!`, no `@ts-ignore` or `@ts-expect-error`, no `as` cast to silence an error. Records are typed in the feature's `model/`.
rules.why: Each escape hatch is a place the compiler stops checking — and the place the next bug comes from.

rules.rule: A module does nothing when it is imported: only declarations at the top level — no registration, no global mutation, no code that runs for its effect. The one exception is a `.css` import. Anything that must run at startup goes in `main.tsx` or `app/providers/`.
rules.why: `package.json` declares `"sideEffects": ["**/*.css"]` so the bundler can drop every export a page does not use. A module that runs code on import would be dropped along with it, and the bug would only show in the production build.

rules.rule: Name files by what they export: components `PascalCase.tsx` with one component per file, hooks `useThing.ts`, everything else `camelCase.ts`. Tests sit next to the file as `<file>.test.ts(x)`.
rules.why: The file name is then the import name, and a test is found by looking next to what it tests.

rules.rule: Every feature ships with tests for its `model/` logic; a page with real behaviour gets a render test using `renderWithProviders`.
rules.why: Model functions are pure, so their tests are cheap and never flaky. They are the ones that catch a wrong total before a customer does.

rules.rule: Do not add a dependency without asking. Never a second router, data-fetching library, state library, HTTP client, date library or UI kit.
rules.why: Every dependency is code you now maintain. Two of the same kind means every engineer has to learn both.

rules.rule: Run `npm run check` (typecheck, lint, format check, tests) and `npm run build`. Both must pass before reporting the work as finished.
rules.why: A change that only works in the dev server has not been checked by anything the CI will run.

rules.rule: Never weaken a check to make it pass: do not disable or downgrade a lint rule, add an `oxlint-disable` comment, loosen `tsconfig`, or edit `.oxlintrc.json`, `tsconfig*.json`, `vite.config.ts` or `AGENTS.md` unless the user asked for that change.
rules.why: These files are the architecture. An agent that edits them to get to green has removed the rule rather than followed it.

rules.rule: Report what was built, how to see it (`npm run dev`, then the route), and which interactions are real and which run on mock data.
rules.why: A demo whose limits go unsaid gets presented as though it has none.

steps: If it belongs in the rail, add a row to `app/layout/navigation.ts`.
Type the records in `model/` first, then the mock data in that shape.
Write the transport in `api/<feature>Api.ts` with the `env.useMocks` branch, then the key factory and hooks in `api/<feature>Queries.ts`.
Export from `index.ts` only what a page will use, and add a test for the `model/` logic.
Point the feature's `api/<feature>Api.ts` at the endpoint. Nothing outside `api/` changes.
If the response shape differs from the mock, fix the type in `model/` and let the compiler list every place that has to change.
In `onSuccess`, invalidate with the feature's key factory — `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: invoiceKeys.all })`.

commands.does: Typecheck, oxlint, oxfmt check and tests — what CI runs.
